tldr: By predicting the next two footsteps of a humanoid robot and cropping only the local terrain patches around them for the reinforcement learning policy, training was accelerated by roughly 3.5× while enabling stable traversal over challenging, unseen terrains and obstacles.
hero_caption: A Unitree G1 humanoid traversing diverse terrains such as stairs, steps, gaps, and narrow corridors zero-shot using an elevation map filtered by a foothold prediction model (FPM). Magenta dots indicate predicted footholds, and green/blue points represent the elevation map sampled around them.
overview:
When controlling robots walking over uneven terrain using visual sensors like cameras, reinforcement learning policies typically take in a dense, robot-centric elevation map of the entire surrounding area. But think about how humans walk. We don't stare at the entire ground around us; we only look at where our next one or two steps will land, adjusting our foot trajectory accordingly. Handing a robot a massive terrain map full of places it will never step forces the policy to learn "what information actually matters" from scratch alongside learning to balance. This drastically slows down training and makes the robot prone to falling when distracted by walls or obstacles irrelevant to its path.

Taking inspiration from human walking strategies, the authors propose filtering the elevation map to focus strictly on the area around the upcoming footholds before the policy sees it. They built a lightweight Foothold Prediction Model (FPM) that predicts the next two footsteps using only proprioception (joint positions, velocities, etc.) and the commanded velocity. The policy is then given just two small terrain patches centered on these predicted footholds. Because the robot's gait changes as the locomotion policy improves, the FPM is periodically retrained from scratch alongside the policy's progress (co-training).

In simulation benchmarks, the proposed method learned to traverse challenging terrains roughly 3.5 times faster than standard full-map approaches. Furthermore, it matched or surpassed computationally heavy attention-based methods while running on a single lightweight GPU setup. In real-world tests using the 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid, the policy achieved zero-shot transfer—cautiously slowing down and traversing out-of-distribution 0.55 m crevices and 0.6 m drop-downs that were never seen during training.
contributions: Proposed a self-supervised Foothold Prediction Model (FPM) that accurately predicts the next two footsteps solely from internal proprioceptive states and velocity commands, periodically updated as the RL gait matures.

Constructed an anticipated perception pipeline that extracts only small patches around predicted footholds from the complete elevation map, drastically reducing input dimensions while focusing on relevant information.
Achieved roughly 3.5× faster training convergence compared to full-map baselines, matching the performance of heavy attention models at a fraction of the computational cost.
Demonstrated zero-shot transfer of a single simulation-trained policy to the real Unitree G1 humanoid, overcoming stairs, large drop-downs, and crevices outside the training distribution.

sections.heading: Walking Like a Human: Looking Only at the Next Steps
sections.summary: Conventional perceptive locomotion processes entire dense elevation maps, leading to poor sample efficiency and distraction from irrelevant terrain. Inspired by how humans focus only 2–3 steps ahead, this work proposes a framework that filters terrain input based on foothold predictions.
sections.details:
Visual perception is essential for bipedal robots walking across rough, uneven terrain. With advances in deep reinforcement learning (RL), feeding a robot-centric elevation map (a 2.5D height grid of the ground around the robot) directly into the policy has become standard practice.

However, this approach suffers from significant waste and vulnerabilities. A walking robot only places its feet on a tiny fraction of the surrounding ground, yet baseline methods feed the entire map into an encoder. When terrain data from the sides or behind the robot—areas it will never step on—are compressed into the policy, it has to learn which spatial regions matter at the same time it learns basic balance, leading to terrible sample efficiency. Furthermore, it faces the problem of visual distraction: extraneous features like walls in narrow corridors can confuse the policy even if the path ahead is clear.

When humans walk, they fixate their gaze roughly 1.5 seconds ahead (about 2 to 3 steps) and ignore the rest of the scenery. If obstacles arise, they adjust leg trajectories mid-air to land safely. Prior robotics works have tried using attention mechanisms to learn where to look, but these are computationally expensive and offer no guarantee that the policy will attend to the right footholds. Meanwhile, manually designing classical foothold planners often clashes with the complex gaits discovered by RL.

To solve this, this research deploys a tiny neural network to predict the next two landing spots before the policy ever sees the elevation map, cropping out only small square patches around those predicted footholds. This prevents the policy from being misled by irrelevant terrain, allowing it to efficiently exploit the ground around candidate landing spots.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation: Simulation and Humanoid Setup
sections.summary: Locomotion is framed as a Markov Decision Process and trained via PPO on IsaacLab using the 29-DoF Unitree G1. The external elevation map is treated separately from the robot's proprioceptive system state.
sections.details:
The locomotion control problem is formulated as a standard Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by state space $\mathcal{S}$, action space $\mathcal{A}$, transition probabilities $P$, reward function $R$, and discount factor $\gamma$.

The simulation environment is built on IsaacLab, running 8,192 parallel environments on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU to train policies with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The target platform is the 29-degree-of-freedom (DoF) Unitree G1 humanoid. The physics engine integrates at 200 Hz, while the control policy is evaluated at 50 Hz.

The robot's proprioceptive system state $\mathbf{x}_t$ consists of the base linear velocity $\mathbf{v}_t$, angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega}_t$, projected gravity vector $\mathbf{g}_t$, user velocity commands $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{cmd}} = (v_x, v_y, \omega_{\mathrm{yaw}})$, and joint positions $\mathbf{q}_t$ and velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}_t$ relative to a nominal stance. Crucially, external terrain information (the elevation map) is excluded from this system state $\mathbf{x}_t$ and handled as a separate observation described below.

sections.heading: Foothold Prediction Model (FPM) and Anticipated Perception
sections.summary: The framework comprises a blind FPM predicting the next two footsteps from proprioception, a patch-sampling mechanism around those predictions, and a co-training schedule that retrains the FPM as the locomotion gait matures.
sections.details:
The proposed architecture consists of two primary components: the Foothold Prediction Model (FPM), which predicts future landing locations, and the locomotion policy, which takes in the cropped terrain patches to output target joint positions (Figure F2).

### III-A Foothold Prediction Model (FPM)
The FPM predicts the horizontal coordinates of the next two footholds, $\hat{\mathbf{p}}_t^1, \hat{\mathbf{p}}_t^2 \in \mathbb{R}^2$, expressed in the current base frame, using only the system state $\mathbf{x}_t$. The key insight here is that the FPM is completely "blind" to the elevation map. If the predictor were fed terrain data, it would inherit the exact computational bottleneck this method aims to avoid. Instead, it infers where the feet will naturally land purely from current body dynamics and intended heading (velocity command).

- Supervision Data: Foot contact sensors record trajectories during policy rollouts. Past states $\mathbf{x}_t$ are paired with the actual relative coordinates of the subsequent two foot touchdown locations as ground-truth labels.
- Loss Function: The model is trained via regression using Huber loss ($\delta=0.01$) to remain robust against outliers.
- Architecture: A remarkably lightweight two-layer MLP with hidden layers $[128, 128]$.

### III-B Foothold-Gated Elevation Sampling
The original elevation map covers a $1.6\,\mathrm{m} \times 1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ area sampled at $0.05\,\mathrm{m}$ resolution, forming a grid of $33 \times 21 = 693$ points. Centered on the two predicted foothold cells, the system extracts two $7 \times 7$ cell patches ($0.35\,\mathrm{m}$ square, ample room for the G1's $\approx 0.208\,\mathrm{m}$ foot length). The elevation values from these patches ($49 \times 2 = 98$ values) concatenated with the predicted coordinates (4 dimensions) result in a compact 102-dimensional visual observation. This achieves an $\approx 85\%$ reduction in input dimensionality compared to the raw 693-point map. To build resilience against prediction errors and odometry drift, random offsets of up to $\pm 0.05\,\mathrm{m}$ are injected into the patch centers during training.

### III-C Co-Training Schedule for Policy and FPM
Early in training, the robot cannot even walk, meaning no meaningful stepping data exists. The first 500 iterations serve as a "bootstrap period" where the policy is simply given patches directly beneath the robot. Every 500 iterations thereafter, the current policy generates rollouts to retrain the FPM from scratch. Retraining from scratch rather than fine-tuning ensures the model quickly sheds immature stepping habits formed during earlier stages.

### III-D Curriculum Learning and Implementation Details
The training curriculum features 10 difficulty levels combining stepping stones ($30\%$), stairs, and boxes. To prevent early falls and allow the robot to learn foot placement adjustments, an upward vertical assist force is applied to the pelvis in initial stages and gradually decayed to zero by difficulty level 4.

Bottom: Every 500 iterations, actual foot touchdowns are extracted from recent policy rollouts to retrain the FPM from scratch.

sections.heading: Experiments: Dramatic Speedups and Robust Real-World Transfer
sections.summary: In simulation, FPM converged roughly 3.5× faster than full-map approaches and matched heavy attention models in traversal success. On the physical Unitree G1, it demonstrated smooth zero-shot traversal over unseen gaps and drop-downs.
sections.details:
To evaluate FPM, the authors compared it against several baselines: full-map input (HM), an ego-centric patch under the feet (Wild), a naive forward crop based on velocity (Naive), a CNN-based map encoder (HM CNN), and a computationally heavy attention-based encoder (AME2).

### IV-A Training Convergence Speed
FPM reached the highest curriculum level fastest, converging in roughly 15,000 iterations. To reach level 5, FPM required only 7,500 iterations, whereas HM took 26,100, HM CNN took 25,200, and Wild took 27,600—a speedup of about 3.4× to 3.5× over full-map baselines. The attention-based AME2 required 20,000 iterations. Moreover, AME2 required 4 GPUs and took 6.3 seconds per policy update, whereas FPM ran on a single GPU in just 0.55 seconds per update—over 10× more computationally efficient.

### IV-B Traversal Performance and Resistance to Distracting Walls
Simulation evaluations tested models on in-distribution terrains, out-of-distribution (OOD) rough ground, and sparse stepping stones. FPM achieved the highest success rate on training terrains ($84.6\%$) and topped sparse stepping stones at $80.2\%$. While AME2 performed similarly on these terrains, a dramatic difference appeared in the "narrow corridor test." In a corridor flanked by high walls, FPM achieved an $89.2\%$ success rate, whereas full-map baselines misidentified the walls as obstacles in their path, collapsing their success rate by more than half. Because FPM filters out the walls entirely, it remained focused strictly on the footholds ahead.

### IV-C Real-World Humanoid Verification (Unitree G1)
The simulation-trained policy was deployed zero-shot onto a physical Unitree G1 across indoor and outdoor environments (Figure F4). The robot reliably climbed and descended 18 consecutive stairs and navigated rubble. Furthermore, when encountering out-of-distribution challenges like a 0.55 m wide crevice or a 0.6 m vertical drop-down, the robot exhibited striking, human-like cautious behavior: it spontaneously slowed down ahead of the edge, lowered its center of mass, and extended its leg carefully before landing.

### IV-D Ablation: How Far Ahead Should the Robot Look?
To assess the prediction horizon, the authors compared looking 1 step ahead (FPM1), 2 steps ahead (proposed FPM2), and 3 steps ahead (FPM3). FPM1 provided too little advance warning, hurting stepping stone success ($62.2\%$ vs. $74.2\%$). On the other hand, in FPM3, the prediction error for the third step ballooned to around 22 cm (roughly the full length of the G1's foot), destabilizing the gait. The analysis revealed that prediction error scales linearly by about 6 cm per step, confirming that a 2-step horizon offers the optimal trade-off between predictive accuracy and look-ahead capability.

captions.F4: Unitree G1 traversing an unseen composite obstacle course zero-shot. It tackles stairs, an out-of-distribution 0.55 m gap, and a 0.6 m drop-down in sequence. As shown in the bottom plot, when approaching large unmodeled drops and gaps, the actual forward velocity (orange) spontaneously drops below the commanded velocity (blue) to execute a cautious crossing.

sections.heading: Discussion and Limitations: Why It Worked and Where It Fails
sections.summary: FPM succeeds by pruning non-essential visual inputs to eliminate distractions. However, it cannot perceive lateral hazards emerging outside the stepping trajectory, and scaling beyond two steps remains difficult.
sections.details:
FPM outperforms full-map methods not merely because of reduced input dimensions. The poor performance of the Naive (fixed forward patch) and Wild (under-foot patch) baselines demonstrates that aligning visual attention with the robot's predicted future steps is what truly matters. Physically pruning irrelevant peripheral terrain also provides built-in robustness against visual distractions like corridor walls.

Nonetheless, clear limitations exist. First, because the policy discards any terrain outside its projected footholds, it is blind to lateral threats—such as sideways obstacles or falling objects approaching from outside its stepping path. Second, the reliable prediction horizon is strictly capped at two steps. Attempting to predict further into the future from current kinematics causes errors to compound due to gait variability and terrain uncertainty, making 3+ step predictions unreliable.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
sections.summary: Anticipated elevation sampling via foothold prediction dramatically streamlines humanoid locomotion learning and enables zero-shot real-world transfer. Future extensions include direct depth-image sampling and whole-body coordination.
sections.details:
This paper presented a lightweight locomotion framework that predicts the next two footsteps from proprioception and velocity commands, feeding only localized elevation patches around those predictions to the RL policy. This setup trains more than 3× faster than full-map baselines, matches heavy attention encoders on a single GPU, and transfers zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1 humanoid.

Looking ahead, the authors aim to move away from precomputed elevation maps toward an active vision system that directly queries depth camera data at the predicted foothold locations. Another promising avenue is extending this foothold-gated attention to whole-body coordination (manipulative locomotion), where contact targets for both hands and feet could be predicted to focus visual processing during climbing and crawling.

takeaways: Flipping the paradigm from "scan everything to find what matters" to "predict footholds from body state and look only there" yields massive improvements in both learning speed and terrain agility.
Physically masking out irrelevant visual inputs fundamentally prevents the policy from being distracted by non-hazardous features like corridor walls.
Blind foothold prediction has a practical limit of two steps ahead (error grows by $\approx 6\,\mathrm{cm}$ per step), which aligns remarkably well with how humans look 2–3 steps ahead when walking.
A lightweight MLP co-training loop matches the traversal performance of expensive attention mechanisms while training quickly on a single regular GPU.
limitations: Because it only samples terrain around anticipated footsteps, the policy cannot detect lateral collision hazards or obstacles falling in from the periphery.
Foothold prediction error grows linearly by about 6 cm per step, preventing simple scaling to long-horizon planning beyond 2 steps.
On structured step terrains like stairs and stacked boxes, full-map baselines retain a slight edge because viewing the entire field makes it easier to perceive overall gradient trends.
